content: Vegetable oils possess fuel properties that are comparable to diesel fuel, but they exhibit higher viscosity and lower oxidative stability. These differences must be addressed to enable vegetable oil to serve as a substitute for 2 diesel fuel, particularly for use in engines or as home heating oil. Failure to do so can result in incomplete combustion, carbon deposits, and eventual engine damage. Enthusiasts often refer to vegetable oil used as fuel as waste vegetable oil (WVO) when it is sourced from discarded restaurant oil, or straight vegetable oil (SVO) to differentiate it from biodiesel. The first documented use of vegetable oil as a fuel occurred in 1900 when an engine built by the Otto company, designed to burn mineral oil, was demonstrated using pure peanut oil at the World's Fair. Rudolf Diesel, the inventor of the diesel engine, later explored the use of vegetable oils as fuel. In a 1912 presentation to the British Institute of Mechanical Engineers, Diesel noted the potential significance of vegetable oils as fuel, predicting that they might one day rival the importance of mineral oils and tar products. Interest in vegetable oil as a diesel substitute has fluctuated over time, often spurred by petroleum shortages. Research into its use gained momentum during the 1930s and 1940s, and again in the 1970s and early 1980s. The 1970s also saw the establishment of Elsbett, a German company that enabled consumers to run their vehicles on straight vegetable oil. During the Bougainville conflict in the 1990s, islanders used coconut oil to fuel vehicles when oil supplies were cut off due to a blockade. However, academic research into straight vegetable oil declined in the 1980s as petroleum prices fell and biodiesel emerged as a more practical alternative requiring fewer vehicle modifications. Although engineers and enthusiasts have experimented with vegetable oil as a diesel engine fuel since 1900, only one peer-reviewed study has compared the long-term effects of vegetable oil and 2 diesel fuel on engine wear. This study, conducted on the German Deutz F3L912W engine, found no significant difference in engine deterioration rates. However, most diesel engines require modifications to use SVO or pure plant oil (PPO). The primary challenge is reducing the viscosity of SVO/PPO, typically achieved by preheating the oil using engine heat or electricity. Without preheating, poor atomization, incomplete combustion, and carbon buildup can occur. A common solution involves installing a secondary fuel tank for conventional diesel fuel (petrodiesel or biodiesel) and a three-way valve to switch between the tanks. The engine is started on diesel, switched to vegetable oil once warmed up, and switched back to diesel before shutdown to prevent vegetable oil from remaining in the engine or fuel lines during a cold start. In colder climates, additional heating of the vegetable oil fuel lines and tank is often necessary to prevent the oil from becoming too viscous or solidifying. Single-tank conversions have been attempted, but these systems often result in significant contamination of the engine's lubricating oil due to blow-by during warm-up. While such systems may function in warm climates with indirect injection (IDI) engines, they are generally unsuitable for other applications. For unmodified engines, blending SVO with diesel fuel can mitigate some adverse effects, but opinions on the effectiveness of this approach vary. Mechanics working with WVO have reported higher rates of wear and failure in fuel pumps and piston rings due to carbonized droplets of partially combusted WVO/SVO. To use vegetable oil in a standard diesel engine without blending or modifications, it must be transesterified into biodiesel. Certain engines, such as those with indirect injection systems and inline or mechanical Bosch injection pumps, can run on pure SVO in all but the coldest temperatures. Pre-common-rail diesel injection (pre-CDI) Mercedes-Benz vehicles and those with PSA XUD engines are particularly well-suited for SVO use, as the latter often includes a coolant-heated fuel filter. In the UK, rapeseed oil (canola oil in North America) is the most commonly used form of SVO, with a freezing point of -10°C. Sunflower oil, which freezes at -17°C, is being investigated for improved cold-weather performance. However, oils with lower gelling points are typically less saturated, leading to higher iodine numbers and increased polymerization in the presence of oxygen. Coconut oil, palm oil, and animal fats like lard and tallow have the highest cetane numbers, indicating superior combustion quality, but they also have low iodine numbers. Some Pacific island nations have adopted coconut oil as a fuel to reduce reliance on imported fuels and stabilize the coconut oil market. Coconut oil is only viable as a fuel in temperatures above 17°C (62°F) unless two-tank systems or other heating methods are employed. Techniques developed for using canola and other oils in cold climates can also be applied to coconut oil to extend its usability in lower temperatures. With minimal modifications, most residential furnaces and boilers designed for 2 heating oil can burn biodiesel or filtered, preheated WVO. While these fuels are not as clean-burning as petroleum-based heating oil, they can offer significant cost savings when processed at home. Many restaurants provide used cooking oil for free or at low cost, and converting it to biodiesel is relatively simple and inexpensive. Burning filtered WVO directly is more challenging due to its high viscosity, but it can be achieved with adequate preheating, making it an economical heating option for those with the necessary technical skills. In 2000, the United States produced over 11 billion liters of waste vegetable oil annually, primarily from industrial deep fryers in food processing plants and fast-food restaurants. If all this oil were collected and used as fuel, it could offset nearly 1% of U.S. oil consumption. However, waste vegetable oil as a fuel competes with other established uses. Pure plant oil (PPO), unlike waste vegetable oil, is not a byproduct of other industries and is limited only by agricultural capacity. For example, the UK exported 280,000 tonnes of rapeseed in 2005. Utilizing set-aside land for rapeseed cultivation could enable the UK to meet its 5% biofuel target without relying on environmentally harmful oil crop imports. In the United States, converting an engine to run on vegetable oil is not legal under Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) guidelines. While the EPA has not penalized individuals for such conversions, regulatory changes or a certification process may be necessary for widespread adoption. Taxation on SVO as a road fuel varies by country. Germany initially offered 0% taxation but began taxing SVO at €0.09 per liter in 2008, with rates increasing to €0.45 per liter by 2012. In the UK, SVO is legal if fuel duty is paid, but drivers have been prosecuted for failing to do so. Recent changes in UK excise duty regulations exempt users of less than 2,500 liters of vegetable oil per year from registration and duty payments. However, the combined cost of SVO and taxation often exceeds the price of mineral diesel, reducing its commercial appeal.
